Availability decides this before quality does: on-device models are free, private and offline, but they exist only on recent hardware, so the server path is the one you must build and the local one is an optimisation you light up when the device says yes.

### What is actually on the device
- **iOS 26+**: the Foundation Models framework exposes Apple's on-device model through `LanguageModelSession` — a few billion parameters, a context window in the low thousands of tokens, guided generation and tool calling, no cost and no network. `SystemLanguageModel.default.availability` tells you whether the hardware is eligible, whether Apple Intelligence is enabled, and whether the weights are still downloading.
- **Android**: ML Kit GenAI wraps Gemini Nano through AICore for fixed tasks — summarize, proofread, rewrite, image description — on a short device list. Anything else means shipping your own weights and running them with LiteRT or MediaPipe's LLM inference API. Firebase AI Logic gives you one API with a hybrid on-device-then-cloud policy.
- Both are small models. Long context, fresh facts and hard reasoning are still a server call.

### How to decide, per feature
- Bounded task, short input, no external knowledge → local first.
- Content that must not leave the device → local, or the feature does not ship.
- Anything where answer quality is the product → server, with local as a degraded offline mode.

Write one interface with two implementations and choose per call, not per app. The trap is treating on-device as a capability rather than a probe: for another couple of years most of your installed base will fail the availability check.

A proxy that forwards whatever body the client sent is an anonymous inference endpoint with your card on file — it has to own the prompt, the model and the budget, not just the secret.

### What the server owns
- The system prompt and the template. The client posts intent and inputs — a thread id, a tone, a locale — never a prompt string. A client that can send prompt text can send any prompt text.
- The model id, the decoding parameters and the token ceiling. Switching vendor or version then costs a deploy instead of a release, and nobody can ask you for the expensive model.
- Quota per authenticated user and per device, with a daily ceiling and a 429 the app can actually render. IP is not an identity on mobile: one carrier NAT is thousands of people.
- Attestation on the path that issues your tokens — Play Integrity, App Attest — so a token scraped off a rooted phone is worth less.
- Per-request token accounting in your own store, tagged with user and feature. The vendor's monthly invoice is not a debugging tool.

### What still has to pass through
- The stream. A proxy that buffers the upstream SSE and answers once at the end has deleted the only thing that made the feature bearable.
- Cancellation. The client closing the connection must abort the upstream call, or you keep paying for tokens nobody will read.
- A request id in the response headers, so a support ticket maps to exactly one generation.

The rule: the client says what the user wants, the server decides what the model is asked and how much of it this user gets.

One token is not one UI update: buffer the deltas and flush on a frame cadence, append into a single text node instead of a growing list of them, and follow the bottom only while the user is already there.

### Why a rebuild per token is not free
- Laying out a growing paragraph redoes the whole paragraph. Eight hundred tokens rendered one at a time is eight hundred layouts of an ever-longer string, and each one costs more than the last.
- Markdown is the hidden half of the bill. Re-parsing the whole buffer on every delta has the same shape; parse on the same cadence, or render finished blocks as Markdown and the trailing line as plain text.
- The fix is to accumulate off the main thread and emit at most every 30-60 ms — `sample()` or `conflate()` on the Flow. Nobody reads faster than that.

### Keeping the list still
- The streaming answer is one list item with a stable key. If it is one item per token, every delta re-measures the viewport.
- Give the bubble a fixed width so growth is vertical only; a paragraph that reflows sideways reads as flicker.

### Scrolling
- Auto-scroll only when the last item is already visible at the bottom, recomputed as derived state rather than remembered as a flag.
- The moment the user scrolls up, stop following and show a jump-to-latest button. Yanking a reader back down on every chunk is the most common complaint about home-made chat UIs.

The mental model: the stream has a data rate, the screen has a frame rate. Convert between them once, at the boundary, and everything above it gets simple.

Cancellation has to reach the socket — closing the response body is what stops the meter — and the partial text already on screen is state, so save it before the scope dies.

### On the client
- The call belongs to the scope that owns the screen. `viewModelScope` dies with the ViewModel; a generation launched on a process-wide scope keeps streaming, and keeps billing, long after the screen is gone.
- Cancelling a coroutine suspended on a Ktor or OkHttp read closes the connection, and that close is the signal. On iOS it is cancelling the `Task` or the `URLSessionDataTask`; checking a cancellation flag stops nothing by itself.
- Persist the partial answer inside `withContext(NonCancellable)`. A cancelled coroutine cannot suspend, so a plain `save()` in a `finally` block is silently skipped — this is the trap that eats half-written answers.
- A cancelled generation is not an error. Show the partial text with a retry, not a red banner.

### What the server needs
- Your proxy must turn a closed client connection into an abort upstream. Forwarding a stream and then forgetting about it means you pay for every token the vendor writes into the void.
- A generation id, so a stop that arrives after the socket is gone still targets something, and so a reconnect can ask about it.
- Its own limits: a max-token cap and an idle timeout. Process death runs no `finally` at all, and from the server side a killed app is indistinguishable from a tunnel. The client's stop is a courtesy; the server's timeout is the mechanism.

Make the final parse a guarantee and treat every prefix before it as layout information only: schema-constrained decoding, a mirror type whose fields are all nullable for the stream, and no value rendered from a token that has not been closed.

### Getting a parse you can trust
- Ask the vendor for constrained output against a JSON schema instead of begging for JSON in the prompt. The last chunk then parses by construction, and a retry loop on `SerializationException` stops being your error handling.
- On iOS 26 the Foundation Models framework does this natively: a `@Generable` type streamed with `streamResponse` yields partially generated snapshots whose properties are optional and fill in declaration order. Order the properties the way you want the screen to fill.
- On the server path you get raw text, so you build the same thing yourself.

### Parsing the prefix
- Decode into a mirror of the real type with every field nullable, using a lenient parser, after truncating the prefix back to its last completed member and closing the containers still open.
- Never take a value out of an unterminated token. A price that reads `12` because the stream stopped mid-`1234` is not a slow number, it is a wrong one.
- Validate against the real, non-null type at the end. A field still missing there is a failure to fall back from, not an empty state to render.

### What the UI shows
- A skeleton shaped like the field — a grey line the height of the title — not one spinner over the whole card.
- Nothing that will change after it appears: never animate a value in and then correct it.
- Actions stay disabled until the object validates, because a button cannot act on half an object.

Persist the conversation as durable turns with ids and treat the ViewModel as a projection of them; on return you ask the server about the generation you already started rather than starting it again.

### What is durable
- Every turn is a row: id, role, text, status (`pending`, `streaming`, `complete`, `failed`), created-at. The screen renders from the store, so process death costs you nothing beyond the last flush.
- Flush the growing assistant text on the same cadence you draw it, not per token.
- Backgrounding is not process death, but it is close enough: an HTTP stream will not survive minutes in the background on either platform, so handle a suspend exactly as you handle a dropped connection.

### What you replay
- On resume, look at the last turn. `complete` needs nothing. `streaming` or `pending` means asking the server about that generation id: a finished one is fetched, a live one is re-attached to, an unknown one becomes `failed` with a retry.
- That requires a server that keeps the result of a generation whose socket died. Without it every lost connection is both a lost answer and a bill you already paid.

### What must never go twice
- The user's turn. Mint its id on the client when the message is created and send it on every attempt, so a retry after a timeout resumes instead of asking again — which matters most when the model can call tools that send, book or pay.
- A truncated assistant turn as context. Replaying half a sentence as if it were finished makes the model continue it; mark it truncated or drop it from the window. And trim that window deliberately — you re-send the transcript every turn, and that is what the bill is made of.

Time to first token is the number the feature lives or dies by: about 100 ms feels instant, a second is fine if something acknowledged the tap, and past a few seconds people leave — while total duration barely matters once tokens are moving, because reading is slower than generation.

### Budget the wait, then measure it
- Split TTFT into your own work, your proxy, and the vendor's queue plus prefill. Usually only one of the three is yours, and it is usually the one nobody instrumented.
- Record TTFT, tokens per second, total duration and cancel rate as separate metrics, at p95, on real networks. An average hides the cold-start tail, and the cancel rate is your honest satisfaction signal.

### Honest ways to feel faster
- Start the request on intent rather than on submit, when the input is already known — the sheet opening, the thread already selected.
- Prompt caching on the server for the fixed system prefix. That is a real prefill saving, not a trick.
- A small fast model for what appears first — a title, a one-line gist — while the large one writes the body.
- Keep an on-device session warm. Loading the weights is most of a local model's first-token cost, and paying it once on screen entry is legitimate.
- Draw the skeleton and enable Cancel immediately, so the wait is visibly a wait with a way out.

### Theatre
- A typewriter animation over an answer you already have in full, deliberately slowed streaming, or invented thinking steps that map to no work. They buy nothing and they cost you the moment somebody notices.
- A determinate progress bar for a generation whose length you do not know is simply a lie. Use an indeterminate indicator and a Cancel that works.

Spend on TTFT, then stop: after the first token you are only racing the user's reading speed.

Weights are content, not code: they ride the platform's asset-delivery channel, they are versioned with the code that reads them, and they are a cache the system may reclaim — so the feature has to work while they are missing.

### Who delivers the bytes
- If the model belongs to the OS — Apple's Foundation Models, or Gemini Nano behind AICore — you ship nothing and store nothing. You query availability, and on Android you may have to trigger a system download and wait the first time.
- Your own weights on Android: an on-demand asset pack through Play Asset Delivery, or Firebase's model downloader with wifi-and-charging conditions. Both give you resume, integrity and a device-side cache you did not have to write.
- On iOS: Background Assets for large packs, which can start at install time and download outside your process, or On-Demand Resources for smaller tagged bundles.
- What you do not do is `GET` a gigabyte into Documents. No resume, no integrity check, it lands in the user's iCloud backup, and a half-arrived file becomes your crash.

### While it downloads
- Unmetered by default, and say the size out loud. Play Asset Delivery hands you a cellular confirmation dialog for large packs; use it rather than spending someone's data plan.
- Version the pack together with its reader. Weights that do not match the tokenizer the binary expects are a crash you will not reproduce.
- The server path is the behaviour before, during and instead of the download.

### Eviction
- iOS purges asset packs and ODR content under disk pressure, silently. The "model is gone" branch is the normal path, not defensive coding.
- Keep your own copies under `cacheDir`, which is excluded from auto backup; nobody's backup quota should hold a gigabyte of re-downloadable bytes.
- Delete on sign-out and when the feature is turned off. A model the user cannot use is a gigabyte you are borrowing.
